name: Aśoka and the Westward Spread of the Dharma
desc:
Aśoka (reigned ca. 268–232 BCE) is the first figure in Buddhist history to leave **material evidence**, and the key figure in pushing Buddhism from a local religion of the Ganges basin toward a religion of Asia.

**Material sources**  The rock edicts and pillar edicts (over thirty survive) were inscribed in several scripts and languages, including Pali, Sanskrit, Kharoṣṭhī, Greek, and Aramaic, and include: the prohibition of killing living beings, tolerance toward all sects, the appointment of "officials of the Dharma", and **a warning against schism in the Saṅgha** — one passage refers directly to "splitting the Saṅgha", the earliest material corroboration of the [[eighteen_schools|schisms of the schools]]. These stone inscriptions are the earliest datable documents in Buddhist history, and their value exceeds that of all later legends.

**Missionary network**  According to the Pali *[[doc_50|Dīpavaṃsa]]*, the *Mahāvaṃsa*, and the edicts, Aśoka sent missionaries to various regions: Mahendra (his son or brother) to Sri Lanka; Majjhantika to Kashmir and Gandhāra; and Soṇa and Uttara to Suvaṇṇabhūmi (roughly present-day Myanmar and Thailand). **The origin of the southern transmission lies here**, while the spread in northwestern India provided the geographical conditions for the flourishing of the Sarvāstivāda and the rise of the Mahāyāna.

**Relation to the councils**  The Theravāda tradition places the third council in Aśoka's time, while the Sarvāstivāda tradition records a separate council under King Kaniṣka — the difference between the two accounts lies not in historical detail but in the era and the royal patron under which each wishes to place the "fixing of the abhidharma basket".

name: The Four Stages of Chinese Translation
desc:
The translation of Buddhist texts into Chinese spanned about eight hundred years (2nd–8th century) and can be divided into four stages — **this is the backbone of the development of Chinese Buddhism**, since the sequence of the Chinese schools is almost the sequence of scripture translation.

**I. Early translation (Eastern Han to Western Jin, 2nd–3rd century)**  An Shigao translated works on meditation and abhidharma (the *Ānāpānasmṛti-sūtra* and others, belonging to the [[sarvastivada|Sarvāstivāda]] system), and Lokakṣema translated the Prajñāpāramitā (the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, 179) — **the two lines of meditation and prajñā were transmitted in parallel from the beginning**. Translators of this period were mostly foreign monks working largely from oral recitation; their style was plain and abounded in [[yichang|matching meanings (ko-i)]].

**II. Kumārajīva and the period between the old and new translations (4th–5th century)**  Kumārajīva (arrived in Chang'an in 401, translated 401–413) produced the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (Zhong lun), *Śataśāstra*, *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*, *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, *Lotus Sūtra* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka), *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, and others, and was renowned for "free translation that conveys the sense"; Madhyamaka and prajñā learning thus truly entered China. Thereafter Paramārtha (6th century) translated the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other works, forming the "old translation" of Yogācāra.

**III. Xuanzang's new translation (7th century)**  Xuanzang (returned to China in 645, translated 645–664) produced the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (646–648), the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (Jushe lun, 651–654), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (660–663), and others, seventy-five works in more than thirteen hundred fascicles in all, and with the *Cheng Weishi Lun* (659) conflated the commentaries of ten masters into a single translation, forming the "new translation" of Yogācāra. **The difference between the new and old translations is not merely verbal** — the same treatise can be read in completely different ways as regards terminology and doctrine, and this is why the Shelun masters and the Faxiang school took separate paths.

**IV. Yijing and the translation of esoteric texts (7th–8th century)**  Yijing (traveled west 671–695, translated after his return) supplemented the Vinaya with the *Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya*; Śubhakarasiṃha (who translated the *Mahāvairocanābhisambodhi-tantra* in 724), Vajrabodhi, and Amoghavajra translated the tantras, and Tang esoterism was established. After this, with the Huichang persecution (845), translation work was interrupted.

**The explanatory power of this periodization**  Setting the founding dates of the schools beside the dates of translation reveals a high degree of synchrony: the translation of the Prajñāpāramitā → the Sanlun school; of the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* → the Tiantai school; of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* → the Huayan school; of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the *Cheng Weishi Lun* → the Shelun masters and the Faxiang school; of the tantras → the Esoteric school. **The sectarian history of Chinese Buddhism is to a large extent a history of scripture translation.**

name: Translation Bureaus and Matching Meanings (Ko-i)
desc:
Scripture translation is not merely a problem of translation but a problem of **how understanding is possible**; two key terms bear on this layer in Chinese Buddhist history.

**Matching meanings (ko-i)** (4th century, associated with Dao'an and Zhu Faya)  Early translators matched Buddhist ideas with the vocabulary of Daoism and Xuanxue: "original non-being" (benwu) for emptiness, "naturalness" (ziran) for the Dharma-nature, and "non-action" (wuwei) for [[nirvana|nirvāṇa]]. This was a necessary transition — without an existing vocabulary, understanding could not begin — but the cost was that **the original meaning was subsumed by indigenous concepts**. Sengrui and Dao'an later reflected on this failing, and Kumārajīva's style of translation was one attempt to correct it.

**Translation bureaus**  From the Yao Qin to the Tang, translation developed from individual oral recitation into a state-level institution: the chief translator (director of translation), the verifier of meaning (who adjudicated doctrine), the verifier of the text (who collated the original), the oral interpreter, the scribe (who recorded), the polisher (who refined the wording), the assistant translators, the editors, and the text polishers worked in a division of labour, dozens of men completing a single work together. Xuanzang's bureau (Ci'en Temple and Yuhua Palace) and Yijing's bureau were the largest, and this institution guaranteed the doctrinal and verbal quality of the translations.

**The five categories left untranslated** (established by Xuanzang, cited in the *Fanyi Mingyi Ji*)  In five cases the transliteration is preserved rather than translated: because it is secret (mantras); because it has many meanings; because no such thing exists here (no counterpart in China); because it follows the ancient (continuing an earlier translation); and because it produces merit (as with bo-re for prajñā, left untranslated rather than rendered "wisdom", so as to preserve respect). This is one of China's earliest **theories of translation**, and also a measure of Buddhism's immense influence on Chinese (a great many words in present-day Chinese, such as shijie "world", yinguo "cause and effect", fannao "affliction", jingjie "realm", yishi "consciousness", danwei "unit", and xianzai "present", derive from the translation of Buddhist texts).

**Why this section matters**  Every characteristic of Chinese Buddhism — the interfusion vocabulary of Tiantai and Huayan, [[chan|Chan]]'s wariness of words, the habit of ko-i-style harmonization — is related to the fundamental situation of "understanding Indian thought through Chinese".

name: Tibetan Translation and the Tibetan Canon
desc:
After Buddhism was introduced to Tibet in the 7th century, translation of scriptures began; in the early 9th century the *Mahāvyutpatti* (a Sanskrit–Tibetan glossary of terms) was compiled and norms for translation vocabulary were established, making the Tibetan translation **the most systematic project of Buddhist scripture translation in history**.

**The two great catalogues and the two canons**  The *Pangtangma*, *Denkarma*, and *Chinphu* catalogues of the earlier diffusion (snga dar) are official registers of translations; translation continued in the later diffusion (from the 11th century), producing the **Kangyur** (the word of the Buddha, i.e. sūtra and vinaya) and the **Tengyur** (the treatises and commentaries, including the works of Indian masters and their exegeses). Compared with the Chinese translations, the Tibetan translations have two characteristics:

- **Quantity and correspondence** — a great many treatises survive in Tibetan but are missing from the Chinese (especially later commentaries on [[hetuvidya|Buddhist logic (hetuvidyā)]], [[madhyamaka|Madhyamaka]], the tantras, and abhidharma), and many are **word-for-word translations**, from which the Sanskrit original can be reconstructed;
- **Uniform norms** — terminology was officially determined and the translation vocabulary was stable, unlike the Chinese, where old and new translations differ enormously.

**The methodology of modern Buddhist studies is therefore the "four-way collation of Sanskrit, Pali, Chinese, and Tibetan"**: for the study of Indian Buddhism (especially Madhyamaka, Buddhist logic, and the tantras), the Tibetan translation is often the only or the most reliable source; for the study of Chinese and East Asian Buddhism, the Chinese translation is the only source.

**The significance of Chinese–Tibetan complementarity**  The two canons complement each other and are the most important resource of modern Buddhist philology: the Chinese preserves treatises translated early whose Indian originals are lost (such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*), while the Tibetan preserves the complete commentarial tradition of the later Indian masters.

name: The Southern Tradition and the Pali Canon
desc:
The transmission of Theravāda Buddhism in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia (Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia), grounded in the Pali canon; it is the only Buddhist tradition today that continues **an earlier form**.

**Establishment of the text**  The Pali canon was first preserved orally in Sri Lanka and, according to the *[[doc_50|Dīpavaṃsa]]*, was first committed to writing in the 1st century BCE (in the time of King Vaṭṭagāmaṇī); thereafter came the systematic commentaries of Buddhaghosa (5th century), whose *[[doc_34|Visuddhimagga]]* organized the whole of practice under the three trainings of ethics, concentration, and wisdom and became the standard treatise of the southern tradition.

**Divergence from the northern transmission**  The southern tradition does not accept the Mahāyāna sūtras or the later treatises, and so has no tathāgatagarbha, no ālaya-consciousness, and no ten-stage bodhisattva system; but it preserves the **details of the precepts and of meditation with exceptional completeness** — for example the full method of practice in the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta*, the analysis of the factors of the four dhyānas and eight concentrations, and the sixteen stages of insight knowledge are all more specific than in the northern transmission.

**The modern insight movement**  In the 20th century the southern tradition developed a vipassanā tradition aimed at laypeople: Mahasi Sayadaw, U Ba Khin, and S. N. Goenka in Myanmar, and Ajahn Chah and the forest tradition in Thailand, among others, simplified the originally monastic meditation methods into courses that could be practised intensively over short periods and spread them throughout the world. **This is the most successful instance of the modern dissemination of Buddhism**, and it has in turn influenced meditative practice in Chinese Buddhism and in the West.

**A common mirror-image misreading**  Calling the southern tradition "Hīnayāna" is a sectarian position and is also inaccurate: the southern tradition calls itself only the Theravāda or the Vibhajyavāda system, and its goals of practice and doctrinal system are not "lesser" — it preserves the complete practice of the three trainings and the Four Noble Truths; only its stance on doctrinal classification differs.
